title: Lipsius and constancy
hookLine: during Europe's religious wars, Justus Lipsius wrote On Constancy (1584)
last: WHOSE HOUSE IS THIS WORD LIVING IN RIGHT NOW.

lines: THE NEWS IS BAD. YOU THINK OF MOVING.
THE SAME KNOT IN THE NEW APARTMENT.
A YOUNG SCHOLAR FLEES THE WAR.
cards: The news is bad, so you think about moving. A new city, a new job, somewhere quieter. Sometimes that's wise.
But sometimes you unpack and find the same knot in your stomach waiting in the new apartment. In his own book, a young scholar from what's now Belgium feels that pull.
His homeland is being torn apart by war, much of it fought over religion, and he packs up to travel to Vienna. On the way, an older friend stops him with a question.

teach.b: First, the book. Justus Lipsius was a Flemish scholar of Latin who edited Seneca and Tacitus. During the religious wars he published a short dialogue called On Constancy.
In it, his younger self, fleeing the turmoil in the Low Countries, stops at Liège and meets a wise older friend named Langius. Second, the question.

teach.h: RUNNING FROM YOUR COUNTRY, OR YOURSELF?
teach.b: Langius asks, in effect: are you running from your country, or from yourself? Changing places won't cure you, because you carry the sickness with you. It's in the mind.
Seneca makes that old Stoic point in his letters; Lipsius set it in his own war. Third, the word.

Langius defines constancy as a steady, upright strength of mind, not lifted up by good fortune or pressed down by bad. It comes from right reason, he says, not from stubbornness or mere opinion. Fourth, the bridge.
Lipsius was a Christian, and he reworked Stoic ideas to fit his faith: where the old Stoics spoke of fate, he speaks of God's providence.
Historians call the movement he helped start Neostoicism. His own life wasn't simple.
He taught at universities on different sides of those divisions, Lutheran, Reformed and Catholic, and his critics called that inconstant; historians still argue over his motives.
But his book gave war-weary readers a plain idea to hold: the storm is out there, and the steadiness has to be built in here.

how: Readers of Lipsius's On Constancy have used it as a guide to keeping a steady mind in public turmoil, blending Stoic ideas with Christian faith in providence.

games.q: you're the young Lipsius, fleeing war at home, stopped at Liège by an older friend. what does he tell you?
o: you're running from yourself; steady the mind instead.
games.why: Langius says a change of place can't cure a troubled mind. constancy has to be built inside.

practice: Think of one storm you're in right now, and notice the urge to escape it, by scrolling, by planning a getaway, by fixing everything at once.
Then feel your feet on the floor and your weight in the chair: not rigid, just upright and steady. Stay there, breathing, while the storm keeps going outside.

wordCard.voice: Neostoicism, the movement Justus Lipsius began by reworking Stoic ideas to fit his Christian faith during Europe's religious wars. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: constancy, steadiness, standing firm. the title of Lipsius's dialogue, De Constantia.

carryVoice: Your line: constancy. The steadiness travels with you, just as the knot did. Day six hundred sixty-one.
